lesson.title: L'Elision Gym
lesson.subtitle: The apostrophe marks a vowel sacrificed — la → l', le → l'

hook.title: French Hates a Vowel Collision
hook.content: Say la opinion fast. Your mouth refuses — two vowels can't share one doorstep. So French cuts the article's vowel and welds the rest: l'opinion. The same happens to le: l'hôtel. The apostrophe isn't decoration; it is a scar where a vowel used to be.

footnotes.title: Not just articles
footnotes.content: je → j'ai (I have), ne → n'aime pas, ce → c'est, de → d'eau. Elision is a general law — wherever a little word meets a vowel, the little word loses its tail.

pattern.title: The Vowel Test
pattern.content: Look at the next word. Does it start with a vowel (or a mute h)? Then the article drops its vowel: l'opinion, l'hôtel, l'eau. Does it start with a consonant? Keep the article whole: la collection, le gâteau. The test is one glance long — and it works for every eliding word in the language.
pattern.trap_note: The tempting wrong move after l'-words: assuming the gender is lost. l'opinion is still la opinion underneath — the it is still la: je la veux.

exercises.explanation: organisation opens with a vowel — la loses its a. One S in French, never a Z.
eau (Latin aqua, all vowels historical scar tissue) is feminine and vowel-initial: l'eau.

exercises.prompt: Add the article: 'the hotel' (hôtel starts with a mute h — same rule as a vowel)
exercises.explanation: The h is written and never said — for elision purposes, l'hôtel behaves exactly like a vowel-initial word.

exercises.idea: I want it — and the it is the opinion
cues: The opinion → l'opinion, but the it stays la
Walk it left: I it want
exercises.explanation: The article elides (l'opinion), but the pronoun doesn't: je la veux. Elision is about collisions — the pronoun stands alone.

diagnosis.cue: je l'veux isn't written French. The article elides only when welded to its noun; the walking pronoun keeps its form: je la veux.

exercises.prompt: Assemble: 'I want the water' (use the partitive-looking piece: de l'eau)

vocab_hints.note: de + l'eau: French counts water like sugar — some water, some sugar

exercises.explanation: de l'eau — 'of the water' is how French says 'some water'. A small preview of the partitive, revisited in topic 13.

summary.outcome: Run the vowel test on sight: vowel-initial noun → l', consonant-initial → la/le — and keep pronouns un-elided.
summary.takeaway: The apostrophe is a vowel's tombstone: la opinion → l'opinion, but the walking pronoun never elides.

twist.prompt: Think it through again without looking back — express "I want it (the opinion)" in French:
twist.explanation: Re-constructing "Je la veux" from the underlying rule cements the pattern of L'Elision Gym.

opinion.etymology_derivation: Latin opinio 'what one supposes'. Starts with a vowel, so la loses its a: l'opinion.

organisation.etymology_derivation: English spells -ization, French -isation — one S, never a Z, in French.

hôtel.shift_rule: Norman doublet: S and H dropped
hôtel.etymology_derivation: Latin hospitalis → hostel AND hôtel — the same word entered English twice: once with its S (hostel, hospital), once without (hôtel).

eau.shift_rule: Latin aqua, all three vowels are ghosts of a
eau.etymology_derivation: Latin aqua → ea → eau: one syllable wearing two vowels and a consonant as historical scar tissue. Feminine: l'eau.

la.etymology_derivation: ille's feminine illa → la. Before a vowel it loses its a: l'opinion.

le.etymology_derivation: Latin ille 'that one' → il → le. English 'the' walked the same road — both are worn-down pointers.

ion.name: The -ION Bridge
ion.phonetic_rule: Spelling converts 1:1; the final N is nasalised — thought, not said (collection /kɔlɛksjɔ̃/).
ion.historical_linguistics: English absorbed thousands of Latin-dress nouns through Norman French and later Renaissance borrowing. The -tion/-sion endings are the single largest cognate landing zone between the two languages.
ion.philological_note: Every -ION noun is feminine, so the article is la — elided to l' before a vowel. The ending is a gender decoder, not a memory item.
ion.literature_source: Walter, Le français dans tous les sens (1988); Pope, From Latin to Modern French (1952).
